ratings.long_description: The thesis is arguable and specific, and every paragraph advances it. The counterclaim is stated fairly and answered with evidence.
The thesis is present but general, or some paragraphs drift. The counterclaim is thin or answered without evidence.
No clear thesis; the essay summarizes the plot. No counterclaim.
At least three well-chosen quotations, accurate, introduced, cited by chapter, and explained.
Quotations are present but dropped in, uncited, or explained only briefly.
Fewer than three quotations, or evidence is inaccurate or missing.
The source is credible, woven into the argument, cited in the text, and correct in Works Cited.
The source is present but stacked beside the argument, or citations contain errors.
No source, or the source is unused or uncited.
Clear introduction, body, and conclusion; transitions guide the reader; MLA format and length met; nearly error-free.
The structure is visible but uneven; some format or length issues; some errors.
The structure is unclear; length or format missing; frequent errors.
An arguable thesis that needs all three texts. Every body paragraph uses at least two texts. The counterclaim is real and fairly stated.
A thesis is present and defended, but some paragraphs handle one text at a time, or the counterclaim is a weak version of the objection.
The essay summarizes each text in turn and asserts a connection in the conclusion.
The source is credible, cited correctly, and changes how at least one moment is read.
The source is relevant but mostly confirms points already made.
The source is missing, not credible, or dropped in without being used.
Specific moments from each text, integrated into the writer's sentences, each followed by an explanation.
Adequate evidence, but some moments are summarized loosely or left unexplained.
Evidence is thin, inaccurate, or unconnected to the claims.
Controlled sentences, comparison transitions, and correct MLA in text and on the Works Cited page.
Generally clear with some awkwardness; citation is present but inconsistent.
Errors interfere with meaning, or citation is largely absent.
A clear thesis stated early, with one specific moment from each of the three texts and the point where they differ.
A thesis is present, but a text is missing or the comparison is asserted rather than shown.
The talk summarizes texts without a thesis.
The source is named and the talk shows how it changed a reading.
The source is named but its effect is vague.
The source is missing.
Audible, paced, 3–5 minutes, spoken rather than read.
Clear but read closely from notes, or slightly over or under time.
Hard to follow, or well outside the time limit.

Dramatic Reading: Give a Master's Prose a Voice
The module's oral performance: pacing, menace, and mood, out loud
🎤 YOUR RECITATION
This module's recitation is prose. Prose has no meter; the music is in pacing (where to slow down and stop), mood (the temperature of the voice), and, in Poe, menace: sounding perfectly polite while meaning something else. Choose one passage below (about a minute of speaking, roughly 120 to 160 words), rehearse it, and record a dramatic reading. Reading from the page is allowed.
📚 CHOOSE ONE PASSAGE (ALL PUBLIC DOMAIN, ALL STUDIED THIS MODULE)
Option A (the marquee): Montresor's opening. The coldest first paragraph in American fiction, printed below. Deliver it as Poe wrote it: calm, reasonable, and chilling precisely because it never raises its voice.

Option B: the last wish, from "The Monkey's Paw." From the moment the knocking begins to the empty road at the end. Your instruments are dread and silence: let the pauses do the knocking.

Option C: the arena, from "The Lady, or the Tiger?" The princess's deliberation, beginning "Her decision had been indicated in an instant" and ending with Stockton's famous final question. Build the weighing in your voice, and hand the question to the listener like a live coal.
OPTION A · THE OPENING OF "THE CASK OF AMONTILLADO" (POE, 1846)
The thousand injuries of Fortunato I had borne as I best could; but when he ventured upon insult, I vowed revenge. You, who so well know the nature of my soul, will not suppose, however, that I gave utterance to a threat. At length I would be avenged; this was a point definitively settled—but the very definitiveness with which it was resolved, precluded the idea of risk. I must not only punish, but punish with impunity. A wrong is unredressed when retribution overtakes its redresser. It is equally unredressed when the avenger fails to make himself felt as such to him who has done the wrong.
Delivery notes: speak it as a confidence to one trusted listener, not a speech. Lean gently on "impunity" and let "I vowed revenge" stay quiet; the quietness is the menace.

Record in one take.

📖 WHAT YOU ARE DOING
Revise your Week 7 draft into a finished original short story, then add a craft reflection paragraph naming the techniques you used and the stories that taught you them.
✎ THE CENTRAL QUESTION
What can a small story hold?
In 1,000 to 1,500 words, put one person in front of a choice that costs something either way, plant details that pay off, let irony do quiet work, and end the story the way you mean to end it: resolved, twisted, or deliberately open.
📝 REQUIRED ELEMENTS · YOUR STORY MUST HAVE ALL SIX
1
Length. A complete short story of 1,000 to 1,500 words. Small on purpose: every scene must earn its place.
2
A protagonist facing a real dilemma. A choice with genuine cost on both sides, the kind Stockton’s princess faces. If one option is obviously right, it is not a dilemma yet.
3
Deliberate foreshadowing. At least two planted details that pay off later, following your Week 5 foreshadowing plan. A first-time reader should feel them; a second-time reader should see them.
4
At least one form of irony. Verbal, situational, or dramatic. Use it in service of the story, the way Poe and Maupassant do, not as decoration.
5
A chosen ending. Resolved (O. Henry), twist (Bierce), or deliberately ambiguous (Stockton). Any of the three can be right; what is graded is that you chose it with intent and built the story to deserve it.
6
Craft reflection paragraph. After the story, one paragraph (150 to 250 words) naming at least three techniques you used, where each appears in your story, and which studied story taught you each one.
✅ ALSO REQUIRED
☐

☐

☐
Your story must be original: your own premise, your own characters, your own sentences. You are borrowing techniques from the masters, never their plots or their words.
☐
End your craft reflection with a short Source Note. See below.
☐
Proofread before you submit.
📝 THE SOURCE NOTE · THREE LINES AT THE END OF YOUR CRAFT REFLECTION

Writers look things up. Before an author sets a story in a mining town in 1890, they find out what a mining town in 1890 was actually like: what the air smelled like, what a shift cost, what people were afraid of. Somewhere in writing your story you almost certainly checked something. Say what it was.

▶
One thing you looked up while writing: a place, an object, a job, a period detail, a word's real meaning.
▶
Where you found it, cited in MLA. If it came from JSTOR, use the Cite option on the article page.
▶
How it changed a detail in your story. If checking it changed nothing, you have not really used it; look up something that matters to a sentence you wrote.
💡 WHAT THIS LOOKS LIKE
“I needed my character to send an urgent message in 1912, so I checked how telegrams actually worked and found that they were charged by the word. That is why her message in paragraph four is so short and strange, and why her brother misreads it. The clipped telegram style became the whole misunderstanding the story turns on.”

Three or four sentences is plenty.

📚 YOUR SEVEN TEACHERS
Every story you studied this module is in the public domain and linked, free, in its reading lesson: The Monkey’s Paw (Jacobs), The Lady, or the Tiger? (Stockton), The Cask of Amontillado (Poe), An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge (Bierce), The Necklace (Maupassant), The Machine Stops (Forster), and The Gift of the Magi (O. Henry). 📋 HOW YOUR STORY WILL BE SCORED

Criterion Strong Developing Beginning

OPTION A · THE SCARLET LETTER, CHAPTER XVII (HAWTHORNE, 1850)

The forest was obscure around them, and creaked with a blast that was passing through it. The boughs were tossing heavily above their heads; while one solemn old tree groaned dolefully to another, as if telling the sad story of the pair that sat beneath, or constrained to forebode evil to come.

And yet they lingered. How dreary looked the forest-track that led backward to the settlement, where Hester Prynne must take up again the burden of her ignominy, and the minister the hollow mockery of his good name! So they lingered an instant longer. No golden light had ever been so precious as the gloom of this dark forest. Here, seen only by his eyes, the scarlet letter need not burn into the bosom of the fallen woman! Here, seen only by her eyes, Arthur Dimmesdale, false to God and man, might be, for one moment, true!

OPTION B · THE SCARLET LETTER, CHAPTER XVII, HESTER SPEAKING

Doth the universe lie within the compass of yonder town, which only a little time ago was but a leaf-strewn desert, as lonely as this around us? Whither leads yonder forest-track? Backward to the settlement, thou sayest! Yes; but onward, too. Deeper it goes, and deeper, into the wilderness, less plainly to be seen at every step; until, some few miles hence, the yellow leaves will show no vestige of the white man’s tread. There thou art free! So brief a journey would bring thee from a world where thou hast been most wretched, to one where thou mayest still be happy! Is there not shade enough in all this boundless forest to hide thy heart from the gaze of Roger Chillingworth?

OPTION C · THE SCARLET LETTER, CHAPTER XVIII

Her sex, her youth, and the whole richness of her beauty, came back from what men call the irrevocable past, and clustered themselves, with her maiden hope, and a happiness before unknown, within the magic circle of this hour. And, as if the gloom of the earth and sky had been but the effluence of these two mortal hearts, it vanished with their sorrow. The objects that had made a shadow hitherto, embodied the brightness now. The course of the little brook might be traced by its merry gleam afar into the wood’s heart of mystery, which had become a mystery of joy.

quizzes.title: Module 5 Intro Survey
quizzes.description:
Module 5: Short Stories

This module asks one question, eight times over: What can a small story hold? A short story has only a few pages to build a world, corner a character, and land an ending. Eight weeks of reading cover foreshadowing, irony, dilemmas, and endings chosen on purpose. The module project is an original short story (1,000 to 1,500 words) plus a craft reflection naming the techniques borrowed and the stories that taught them.

Reading roadmap: Week 1 is the writer's toolbox (the literary terms). Then one story per week: The Monkey's Paw (W. W. Jacobs), The Lady, or the Tiger? (Frank R. Stockton), The Cask of Amontillado (Edgar Allan Poe), An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge (Ambrose Bierce), The Necklace (Guy de Maupassant), The Machine Stops (E. M. Forster), and The Gift of the Magi (O. Henry).

Every story is in the public domain and linked in its reading lesson (Project Gutenberg / Wikisource).

questions.text:
First answer.

What can a small story hold? What can a story of only a few pages do to a reader that a long novel cannot? Write 3–4 sentences. The question is answered again at the end of the module.

An ending that stayed with you.

Name a story ending that stuck with you (a book, a film, an episode). Was it neatly resolved, a twist, or left deliberately open? Explain in 2–3 sentences why that ending choice worked.

Objectives acknowledgment.

This module covers seven classic short stories, a recorded dramatic reading, and an original short story (1,000 to 1,500 words) with a craft reflection built step by step through five project feeders. Have you reviewed the module objectives and the project?

quizzes.title: Module 6 Intro Survey
quizzes.description:
Module 6: The Scarlet Letter

This module asks one question across five weeks: What does a community owe the person it judges, and what does a person owe the truth? Nathaniel Hawthorne’s The Scarlet Letter (1850) follows Hester Prynne, a woman made to wear a scarlet A in Puritan Boston, and the people whose choices surround her. Your module project is a literary analysis essay (900 to 1,200 words, MLA format) that makes an argument about the novel and uses one researched source beyond it. Three project feeders (a source note, a thesis with evidence, and an outline) lead into the essay.

Your reading roadmap: Week 1, Chapters I–VI (the prison-door, the scaffold, Chillingworth’s oath, Hester’s needlework, and Pearl). Week 2, Chapters VII–XII. Week 3, Chapters XIII–XIX. Week 4, Chapters XX–XXIV. Week 5, the whole novel and the essay.

A note on your books: The Scarlet Letter is in the public domain. It is free to read online and is linked in each lesson. You do not need to buy anything for this module. Optima course materials are original instructional materials designed to support analysis, discussion, and assessment of the work.

questions.text:
Your first answer.

Before reading the novel: What does a community owe a person it judges? What does a person owe the truth? Write 3–4 sentences. The same question returns at the end of the module.

A judgment you remember.

Think of a book, film, or show in which a community judged one of its own members. Name it and explain in 2–3 sentences whether the judgment seemed fair and why.

Objectives acknowledgment.

This module asks you to read a 19th-century novel in five weeks, practice participial phrases, semicolons, and other sentence tools, and write a 900–1,200-word literary analysis essay with one researched source, built through three project feeders. Have you reviewed the module objectives and the project?

answers.text: ( ) Yes: I have reviewed the objectives and I am ready to begin. (correct/expected)
( ) Not yet: I will review them before the first lesson.

Module 6: Closing the Loop on The Scarlet Letter

You have read the novel, followed the letter through its changing meanings, researched Puritan New England, and written a literary analysis essay. In the module intro you gave a first answer to the question what does a community owe the person it judges, and what does a person owe the truth? Now answer it again, as a reader who has argued it. This survey is reflection, not a test.

questions.text:
The central question, revisited.

At the start of the module you gave a first answer to what does a community owe the person it judges, and what does a person owe the truth? Answer it again in 4–5 sentences. How has your thinking changed, and what changed it: a scene in the novel, your research, or writing the essay?

quizzes.description:
Module 7: The Crucible

This module asks one question: When a community turns fear into law, what becomes of justice, loyalty, and conscience? Arthur Miller's play looks back to Salem in 1692 and speaks to the American 1950s. Over four weeks the module covers the play, its history, and its connections to the texts read this year. The module project is a cross-text essay (900 to 1,200 words, MLA) that traces one theme (justice, loyalty, family, or duty) across The Crucible and at least two earlier course texts, with one researched source, followed by a recorded presentation of 3 to 5 minutes.

Your reading roadmap: Week 1 is Salem in 1692, Miller's moment, and Act One. Week 2 is Act Two and the start of your research question. Week 3 is Acts Three and Four. Week 4 is the review of the year's texts and the building of your argument.

discussions.title: Week 1 Discussion: Every Story Is a Fight
discussions.html:
Every story is a fight. Prove it with one you know.

This week you learned that conflict is the engine of plot and that the climax is the moment the conflict is decided, not just the most exciting scene.

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

  1. Choose a story you know well: a novel, a short story, a film, or a game with a real story.
  2. Name its central conflict and label the type (person vs. person, self, nature, or society). If the story layers an outer and an inner conflict, name both.
  3. Identify the climax and defend your choice: explain why this moment is where the conflict is decided, and name one exciting scene that is not the climax and why it doesn't qualify.
  4. Bonus move: point out one setting or point of view choice that makes the conflict stronger.

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): pick someone who analyzed a different conflict type than you did. Test their climax choice: do you agree that the conflict is decided there? If not, propose a different moment and say why. Disagree with the idea, not the person.

Note: spoilers are allowed and expected. Analyzing endings is the whole point this week.

discussions.title: Week 2 Discussion: Did the Whites Bring It on Themselves?
discussions.html:
Did the Whites bring it on themselves?

Sergeant-Major Morris warns the Whites three separate ways: he tells them the fakir enchanted the paw "to show that fate ruled people's lives, and that those who interfered with it did so to their sorrow"; he reveals that the first owner's third wish "was for death"; and he throws the paw on the fire with his own hands. The Whites wish anyway. By the end, Herbert is dead, something has knocked at the door in the night, and the road stands quiet and deserted.

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

  1. Take a position: were the Whites the authors of their own ruin, innocent victims of fate (or of the paw), or something in between?
  2. Cite one specific moment from the public-domain text (The Monkey's Paw at Project Gutenberg Australia). Name who is speaking or acting, and quote a short line.
  3. Explain in a sentence or two how that moment supports your position. (Strong posts wrestle with the hard part: the Whites were warned, but the warnings were also easy to laugh at on a cozy evening.)

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): respond to someone who took a different position, or who used different evidence. Push the conversation forward: add a reason, raise a question, or point to a moment they did not consider. Be courteous; disagree with the idea, not the person.

Note: the story is deliberately ambiguous about whether the paw has any power at all. You may use that ambiguity as evidence for either side.

discussions.title: Week 3 Discussion: Which Door?
discussions.html:
Which came out of the opened door: the lady, or the tiger?

Stockton refused to answer his own question for the rest of his life. That does not mean all answers are equal. Answer it the way a careful reader does: from evidence in the text, not from preference. "I like dark endings" is not evidence; "she had gnashed her teeth, and torn her hair" is.

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

  1. State your verdict clearly: the lady or the tiger.
  2. Cite one specific moment from the public-domain text (en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Lady,_or_the_Tiger?). Name the moment and quote a short line.
  3. Explain in a sentence or two how that moment supports your verdict, and why it outweighs the other side.
  4. Concede the strongest piece of evidence against you, and answer it in one sentence. (This is the claim, weigh, concede move from the character-motivation lesson.)

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): find someone who chose the other door, and push on their evidence: is their quoted moment doing the work they say it does? Add a moment they did not consider, or a question their reading has to answer. Be courteous; disagree with the reading, not the reader.

Note: it is fine to change doors here if a classmate's evidence convinces you; changing your mind for a reason is the skill.

discussions.title: Week 4 Discussion: Does Montresor Get Away With It?
discussions.html:
Does Montresor get away with it?

On the surface, yes: "For the half of a century no mortal has disturbed them." No court finds him, no punishment falls, and the story ends with a funeral blessing from the murderer's own mouth: In pace requiescat! ("May he rest in peace.")

But look closer, using Montresor's own two rules from the opening paragraph: the avenger must punish with impunity, and must make himself felt as such to him who has done the wrong. Fifty years later, an old man is still telling this story to someone who "so well knows the nature" of his soul, still explaining that his sick heart was only the dampness of the catacombs, and the insult that justified everything is never named, to Fortunato or to us.

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

  1. Take a position: does Montresor get away with it: fully, partly, or not at all? Measure the deed against his own two rules, not just against the law.
  2. Cite one specific moment from the public-domain text (en.wikisource.org: The Cask of Amontillado, 1850 Works text/Volume_1/The_Cask_of_Amontillado)). Quote a short line and name where it falls in the story.
  3. Then answer the second question: what does the last line suggest? Is "In pace requiescat!" a boast, a final stroke of verbal irony, or something closer to a prayer from a man confessing at the end of his life? Commit to a reading and give one reason from the text.

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): find someone who read the last line differently, or who scored the "getting away with it" question differently, and engage their evidence: what does their reading explain well, and what does it have trouble explaining? Be courteous; disagree with the reading, not the reader.

Note: this is also the course's justice question from Module 1 in a new setting; bringing Electra into your reply is allowed.

discussions.title: Week 5 Discussion: When Did You Know?
discussions.html:
Bierce's ending only works because the escape was never real. On a first reading, when did you first suspect something was wrong with Farquhar's escape? And once you knew, which details turned out to be Bierce warning you all along?

A good twist rewards a reader twice: once with surprise, and once on the reread, when the clues were there in plain sight. Argue from the text, not from the feeling of being fooled.

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

  1. Name the exact moment in Part III where you first doubted the escape was real. Quote a short line from that moment (en.wikisource.org/wiki/An_Occurrence_at_Owl_Creek_Bridge).
  2. Point to one detail Bierce planted that, on a reread, signals the escape is imagined (for example, the too-sharp senses, the swelling tongue, the pain, the strange stillness). Quote it and explain how it works as a warning.
  3. Say in a sentence or two whether you think the twist plays fair. Does Bierce cheat the reader, or does he tell the truth quietly and let us miss it?

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): find a post that named a different "first doubt" moment than yours, and add to it. Did they catch a signal you missed, or did you catch one they did? Be courteous; build on the reading, do not just agree.

The story-time chart and the time-distortion marks from the first Owl Creek lesson are usable evidence for this post.

discussions.title: Week 6 Discussion: Fate or Choice?
discussions.html:
Maupassant's first sentence blames "a mistake of destiny." By the end, the Loisels have lost ten years. Was their ruin the work of fate, or the sum of choices they could have refused? Take a side and defend it from the text.

Both sides have textual evidence. Build the stronger case, and be honest about what the other side gets right.

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

  1. Take a clear position: fate, choice, or a defensible mix (and if a mix, say which matters more).
  2. Support it with at least two specific moments from the public-domain text (en.wikisource.org/wiki/Stories_by_Foreign_Authors_(French_I)/The_Necklace/The_Necklace)). Quote short lines.
  3. Name the single moment where you think the story could have turned out differently (the one honest sentence that would have cut the chain), and say who could have spoken it.
  4. Connect it to this course's running question since Module 1: what do we owe each other? What does this story add to that question?

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): find a post that took a different side than yours and test it. Where is their reading strongest, and where does the text push back? Be courteous; argue with the reading, not the reader.

The ledger and the fork diagram from the Necklace lessons are usable evidence here.

discussions.title: Week 7 Discussion: What Did Forster Get Right About 2026?
discussions.html:
In 1909, E. M. Forster imagined people living alone in rooms, seeing each other through glowing plates, and having everything delivered by a machine. What did he get right about 2026?

"He predicted the internet" is not enough. Argue from the text, not from vibes: "the story feels like today" is not evidence; a quoted line set beside a specific, named feature of life in 2026 is.

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

  1. Choose one specific detail from the public-domain text (en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Machine_Stops): quote a short line and say where in the story it appears.
  2. Name its closest real counterpart in 2026 as precisely as you can. Not "phones," but the exact habit, feature, or system the line matches.
  3. Explain in a sentence or two how far the match goes: what the story got exactly right, and where the comparison starts to stretch.
  4. Then name one thing Forster got wrong about a machine-mediated future, and support that from the text too. (A prophecy's misses are as instructive as its hits.)

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): find a post built on a different detail than yours, and test the match: does their quoted line really predict what they say it predicts? Push the comparison one step further, or one step back. Be courteous; disagree with the reading, not the reader.

Readers a century from now will judge a story's world the same way; keep your answer to Question 4 in mind when revising your own story.

discussions.title: Week 8 Discussion: The Ending That Earns Its Meaning
discussions.html:
O. Henry ends "The Gift of the Magi" on a double irony: Della sells her hair to buy Jim a watch chain; Jim sells his watch to buy Della combs. It could be bleak. Instead it lands as warmth. How does O. Henry make a twist ending feel earned rather than like a trick, and what does that teach you about the ending of your own story?

Across this module you have met four kinds of ending: Bierce's twist (Owl Creek Bridge), Stockton's deliberate ambiguity (The Lady, or the Tiger?), Maupassant's bitter situational irony (The Necklace), and now O. Henry's warm situational irony. This week you choose one on purpose for your own story. Argue from the text, then turn the lens on your draft.

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

  1. Quote the moment in "The Gift of the Magi" where the double irony lands (the public-domain text), and name what makes it feel warm rather than cruel. Point to the narrator's own comment on the "wisest" gift-givers.
  2. Compare it to one other ending from this module (Bierce, Stockton, or Maupassant). What does O. Henry do differently to earn his effect?
  3. Name the ending you are choosing for your own story (resolved, twist, or deliberately ambiguous) and explain in a sentence or two why that ending is right for the story you built.

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): read the ending they chose for their own story and give one honest, useful response. Does the ending they describe seem earned by what they have planted, or would a reader feel tricked? Suggest one small thing that would make it land. Be courteous and specific; this is a workshop, not applause.

Quoted examples of the endings studied are usable evidence here and in the craft reflection.

discussions.title: Week 1 Discussion: Who Is on the Scaffold?
discussions.html:
Who is on the scaffold?

In Chapters II and III, Hester Prynne stands on the platform of the pillory. Others stand elsewhere: the governor and the ministers on the balcony above, the crowd in the street below, and a stranger at the edge of the crowd who remarks that “the partner of her iniquity should not, at least, stand on the scaffold by her side.” The community has decided that one person stands where all can see her.

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

  1. Take a position: does the judgment belong to Hester alone, or does someone else belong on the scaffold with her? Name who, and why.
  2. Cite one specific moment from Chapters I–VI (The Scarlet Letter at Project Gutenberg). Name who is speaking or acting and quote a short line.
  3. Explain in a sentence or two how that moment supports your position.

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): respond to someone who took a different position or used different evidence. Add a reason, raise a question, or point to a moment they did not consider. Disagree with the idea, not the person.

discussions.title: Week 2 Discussion: What Is Chillingworth Owed?
discussions.html:
What is Chillingworth owed?

Roger Chillingworth begins his search for Hester's partner, in the narrator's words, “with the severe and equal integrity of a judge, desirous only of truth”. The question involves “wrongs inflicted on himself”. By Chapter XI the narrator describes “a quiet depth of malice” and calls him “more wretched than his victim”. Hester, bound by her oath, stays silent about who he is.

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

  1. Take a position: Is Chillingworth owed anything (the truth, an apology, justice, revenge), and does what he does with it change what he is owed?
  2. Cite one specific moment from Chapters IX–XII (The Scarlet Letter at Project Gutenberg): name who is speaking or acting, and quote a short line.
  3. Explain in a sentence or two how that moment supports your position.

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): respond to someone who took a different position, or who used different evidence. Add a reason, raise a question, or point to a moment they did not consider. Be courteous; disagree with the idea, not the person.

Note: the narrator's judgment of Chillingworth is part of the evidence. A post may accept it or argue against it.

discussions.title: Week 3 Discussion: Should Hester and Dimmesdale Flee?
discussions.html:
Should Hester and Dimmesdale flee?

In Chapter XVII Hester asks, “Is the world, then, so narrow?” and urges Dimmesdale to leave by forest-track or by sea. Dimmesdale answers that he is powerless to go: “I dare not quit my post”. In Chapter XVIII the narrator frames his decision as a choice “between fleeing as an avowed criminal, and remaining as a hypocrite”. The plan ends in Chapter XIX with the letter back on Hester’s breast.

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

  1. Take a position: should they flee, should Dimmesdale stay and confess, or is neither choice enough?
  2. Cite one specific moment from Chapters XVI–XIX (Chapter XVII, Chapter XVIII, or Chapter XIX). Name who is speaking or acting, and quote a short line.
  3. Explain in a sentence or two how that moment supports your position, and what the person owes: the truth, the town, or Pearl.

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): respond to someone who took a different position, or who used different evidence. Add a reason, raise a question, or point to a moment they did not consider.

discussions.title: Week 4 Discussion: What Does the A Mean at the End?
discussions.html:
What does the A mean at the end?

Hawthorne closes the novel with several accounts of the scaffold scene and then says, “The reader may choose among these theories.” By the final pages, the letter has moved from shame toward something else: “the scarlet letter ceased to be a stigma which attracted the world’s scorn and bitterness, and became a type of something to be sorrowed over, and looked upon with awe, yet with reverence too.” The last words of the book are a tombstone motto about the letter A.

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

  1. Take a position: at the end of the novel, does the A mean shame, guilt made honest, or something else?
  2. Cite one specific moment from Chapter XXIII or Chapter XXIV of the public-domain text. Name who is speaking or acting, and quote a short line.
  3. Explain in a sentence or two how that moment supports your position.

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): respond to someone who took a different position, or who used different evidence. Add a reason, raise a question, or point to a moment they did not consider. Disagree with the idea, not the person.

discussions.title: Week 5 Discussion: Hawthorne’s Verdict
discussions.html:
What is Hawthorne’s verdict?

In Chapter XXIV the narrator offers a moral, “Be true! Be true! Be true!” and, about the mark on Dimmesdale’s breast, says “The reader may choose among these theories.” The narrator also reports that Hester returned and resumed the letter “of her own free will”.

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

  1. Take a position: whom does Hawthorne judge most severely: the community, Hester, or Dimmesdale?
  2. Cite one specific moment from the novel (The Scarlet Letter at Project Gutenberg), name the chapter, and quote a short line.
  3. Explain in a sentence or two how that moment supports your position.

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): respond to someone who took a different position or used different evidence. Add a reason, raise a question, or point to a moment they did not consider.

discussions.title: Week 1 Discussion: Who Benefits from an Accusation?
discussions.html:
Who benefits from an accusation?

In Act One, Abigail, Parris, and the Putnams each have something to gain or lose when the village decides that witchcraft is the cause of the girls' behavior. Each of them also has something to fear.

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

  1. Choose one character from Act One and state what that character gains from an accusation, and what the character risks without one.
  2. Cite one specific moment from Act One, named by who acts and what happens.
  3. Explain in a sentence or two how that moment shows the character's motive.

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): respond to someone who chose a different character, or who read the same moment differently. Add a reason, raise a question, or point to a moment they did not consider.

discussions.title: Week 2 Discussion: Is Proctor's Silence a Lie?
discussions.html:
Is Proctor's silence a lie?

In Act Two, John Proctor knows from Abigail herself that the girls' accusations began as pretense. He has told Hale and Elizabeth, but he has not told the court. Telling the court would mean admitting the affair, and no one else heard Abigail say it. Meanwhile the court arrests Elizabeth.

In your initial post (about 5-7 sentences):

  1. Take a position: is withholding what he knows the same as lying, a different wrong, or a fair choice given what it would cost him?
  2. Cite one specific moment from Act Two in your copy of The Crucible. Give the act, name who is speaking or acting, and describe what happens. A short quotation is acceptable.
  3. Explain in a sentence or two how that moment supports your position.

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3-4 sentences): respond to someone who took a different position, or who used different evidence. Add a reason, raise a question, or point to a moment they did not consider. Disagree with the idea, not the person.

discussions.title: Week 3 Discussion: Proctor and Hester
discussions.html:
Proctor and Hester

In Chapter III of The Scarlet Letter, the crowd and the clergy demand that Hester Prynne name the father of her child. She answers in front of the whole town: “I will not speak!” answered Hester, turning pale as death, but responding to this voice, which she too surely recognized. “And my child must seek a heavenly Father; she shall never know an earthly one!” (Chapter III at Project Gutenberg).

In Act Four of The Crucible, Danforth demands that John Proctor name others he saw with the devil, and then demands that his signed confession be posted for the town to read. Proctor refuses both.

In your initial post (about 5-7 sentences):

  1. Take a position: is refusing to name names an act of loyalty, an act of conscience, or both?
  2. Use one moment from each text: quote Hester's line from the public-domain text, and describe one moment from Act Four in your own words, naming the act.
  3. Explain in a sentence or two how the two moments together support your position.

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3-4 sentences): respond to someone who took a different position, or who used different evidence. Add a reason, raise a question, or point to a moment they did not consider. Disagree with the idea, not the person.

discussions.title: Week 4 Discussion: What Is a Name Worth?
discussions.html:
What is a name worth?

In Act Four, Proctor is offered his life in exchange for a signed confession. He signs, then refuses to let the paper be displayed, and he goes to the gallows. Elsewhere in the year's reading, other characters make their own trades: Hester carries a public mark for years, and Gawain returns to court wearing a token of his failure.

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

  1. Take a position: was Proctor right that his name was worth more than his life, wrong, or is the question unfair as stated?
  2. Cite one specific moment from Act Four of your own copy of The Crucible (name who acts and what happens; paraphrase, or quote briefly with the page number), and one moment from an earlier course text that bears on the same question.
  3. Explain in a sentence or two how the two moments support your position.

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): respond to someone who took a different position, or who chose different evidence. Add a reason, raise a question, or point to a moment they did not consider. Be courteous; disagree with the idea, not the person.
